lines.text: Pizza Hut built its empire on dining rooms, Domino's built a machine for your doorstep, and that one difference cost the king of pizza its crown.
In 2015, Pizza Hut was still number one. It held 16.9% of the American pizza market. Domino's was behind it, with 14.2%.
What happened? Ten years later, the numbers had flipped. Domino's had climbed to 23.4%, and Pizza Hut had sunk to 12.1%.
And in 2026, the company that owned Pizza Hut sold the whole chain, for $2.7B. Two buyers split it between them.
By then, hundreds of red roofs had already gone dark. Many still stand, selling something else.
This is the pizza war. So how did the king of American pizza lose its crown to a delivery shop from Michigan?
It wasn't one bad pizza, or one bad ad. It was a choice made decades earlier, about where people would eat.
One chain built restaurants for sitting down. The other built a machine for getting pizza to your door.
This is the pizza war, from the companies' filings and reporting: the red roofs, the delivery promise, the confession, the app, the closures, the sale, and the one country where Pizza Hut still wins.
Pizza Hut was the king. This is how Domino's took the crown.
Chapter one. The red roof, and how two students in Kansas built the king of pizza.
The first Pizza Hut opened in 1958, in Wichita, Kansas, in a small brick building on a busy street corner.
Two brothers started it, Dan and Frank Carney, students at what was then the University of Wichita. What did two students know about running restaurants? Enough.

They sold their first franchise within a year. Other owners put up the money and the buildings, and the Pizza Hut name went up on the sign. That is how two students turned one small restaurant into a national chain.
Within a year, the first franchise opened. Decades later, the company's own annual report still told it the same way.
Today the original little brick building is a museum, moved onto the university's campus.
As the chain spread, one thing made every restaurant easy to spot. The filing says it plainly: the distinctive decor features a bright red roof.
You could see it from the highway: in Oregon, in Florida, in California, in Indiana.
Inside, you sat down. Waiters, tables, booths, and pizza brought to you in a pan.
Going out for pizza meant the whole family in the car, a table by the window, and an evening out. For decades, that was the business, and it worked.
Its filings listed its pizzas by name. Pan Pizza was the famous one. But one more on that list matters later in this story: Stuffed Crust.
How big did it get? By 1977 there were nearly 3,200 Pizza Huts. That year, PepsiCo bought the chain, and it kept building more.
In 1984, Pizza Hut started BOOK IT!, a reading program that rewarded children with pizza.
It still reaches over 14M students a year, according to the Pizza Hut Museum. For many kids, the red roof was their first restaurant.
Pizza Hut was everywhere. By 1997, it had more than 8,600 restaurants in the United States alone.
That's the line in the annual report, right under the red roof.
And it went abroad early. By then, the red roof had more than 3,800 restaurants outside the United States, from Britain to Asia.
That same year, PepsiCo spun its restaurants off into a new company. It was later renamed Yum Brands. The new company owned three big chains, and Pizza Hut was one of them.
Pizza Hut now sat beside KFC and Taco Bell, in the biggest restaurant group of its kind.
Year after year, its filings called Pizza Hut the largest restaurant chain in the world specializing in ready-to-eat pizza.
It was built for families who drove to a red roof and sat down. But in Michigan, a man was building something very different. What if you never had to leave the house at all?
Chapter two. The delivery machine, built in Michigan for one job only.
In 1960, the Monaghan brothers borrowed $900 and bought a small pizza store in Ypsilanti, Michigan.
It became Domino's Pizza in 1965. The first franchise opened in 1967.
Domino's never built big dining rooms. Its stores were small, built for two jobs: delivery and carryout.
The difference sounds small. It wasn't. A dining room needs land, parking, waiters and a long lease. A delivery store needs an oven, a phone, and a few drivers.
And a delivery store can sit almost anywhere: in a strip mall, beside a laundromat, a few streets from the houses it serves. Nobody needs to see it from the highway.
Its filing put it bluntly. Its store model was an advantage over competitors who focus on many parts of pizza, particularly dine-in. Why fight over tables, when the customer is at home?
And it made a promise that every customer remembered: your pizza in thirty minutes or less. For a delivery company, speed was the whole product.
What could stop a promise like that? A courtroom. In 1993, a jury in St. Louis awarded $78M in punitive damages to a woman hurt when a Domino's driver ran a red light.
Less than a week later, Domino's dropped the thirty-minute guarantee.
But it kept what mattered: thousands of small stores, all built around one job, getting a pizza out the door. No booths to clean, no waiters to pay, no big rent on a dining room.
In 1998, an investor group led by Bain Capital bought a 93% controlling stake from Tom Monaghan and his family, and Monaghan retired. In 2004, Domino's went public.
By then, Domino's already had over 6,200 stores, more than 1,700 of them outside America, on six continents.
It took that model around the world: to Europe, to Japan, to India, to China.
A Domino's in Tokyo looks like a Domino's in Bengaluru: a counter, an oven, and a line of scooters.
Abroad, the machine barely stumbled. By the end of 2008, sales at its international stores had grown for 60 quarters in a row.
By the start of 2010, it had 8,999 stores in more than sixty international markets.

By the late two-thousands, Domino's had the stores, the drivers and the scooters. But it had one problem nobody could deliver away. People didn't like the pizza. How do you fix that, when millions already think your pizza is bad?
Chapter three. The confession: the day Domino's said its own pizza was bad.
In 2008, sales at Domino's existing US stores fell 4.9%. The stores were fine. The drivers were fast. The problem was what was inside the box.
Customers had a word for the crust. When Domino's later put their complaints into its own ads, one word flashed across the screen: cardboard. Would any company really put that on television?
So in 2009, Domino's threw out its core pizza and started again: new sauce, new crust, new cheese.
Its next annual report says it simply: the launch of our improved pizza recipe, with a campaign called Oh Yes We Did.
It even put up a website, pizza turnaround dot com, to show the changes and to collect what customers thought of the new pizza.
It was a huge risk. Telling millions of people your pizza was bad could have driven them away for good. Instead, they came back to try it.
Here's the strange part. Domino's built the ads around how bad its old pizza was. The head of its US business, Patrick Doyle, soon to be its chief executive, appeared, saying it was time to change.
TIME magazine called it brutal truth in advertising. But did customers actually come back?
It worked. In 2010, sales at Domino's existing US stores jumped 9.9%.
From a fall of 4.9% to a rise of 9.9%, in two years, with the same stores and the same drivers.
And TIME reported something Domino's hadn't seen in years. In 2010, its number of US stores grew again, for the first time since 2007.
Pizza Hut, meanwhile, still had thousands of big dining rooms to heat, staff and pay rent on.

Domino's had fixed the pizza. Next, it would change how people ordered it, and that's where the war was really won. How do you beat a rival with thousands of restaurants? You make the restaurant unnecessary.
Chapter four. The pizza company that became a tech company, one order at a time.
In 2007, Domino's introduced Pizza Tracker. You could watch your order move, step by step, from the oven to the car.
Why did a progress bar matter? Because waiting is the worst part of delivery, and Domino's turned the wait into something you could watch.
Each order through the app skipped the phone call. And the app was always in people's pockets, one tap away from a pizza.
By 2017, more than half of all its sales worldwide came from digital orders, on its website and its apps. A pizza chain was now selling more online than over the counter or the phone.
Its own filing even made a bolder claim: among the largest e-commerce retailers, by transactions.
And that same year, Domino's passed Pizza Hut as America's biggest pizza chain. The delivery shop from Ypsilanti was now the king.
And the other big chains? Over the same ten years, Papa John's share barely moved. This was a two-company war, and Domino's gained more than Pizza Hut lost.

Then it did something that looked like madness. It opened new stores close to its own stores. Why would anyone do that? The filing calls it fortressing. On paper, it meant its own stores would steal each other's customers. In practice, it worked.
Smaller delivery areas meant hotter pizza and faster drivers. More stores meant more people near enough to walk in and carry out.
It isn't risk-free. Domino's own filing warns that fortressing can close stores if it goes too fast, as it has in some markets abroad.
By 2025, more than 85% of Domino's US sales came through digital orders. Phone calls had become the exception.
Its own filing says that by 2025 it led both halves of the business: about 32.9% of American pizza delivery, and 19.6% of carryout.
And its stores? Its filing says most of them do not offer a full-service dine-in experience. They never needed to.
Domino's was built for the phone, then the website, then the app. Pizza Hut was built for the parking lot. And the parking lots were emptying.
So far: Pizza Hut built the red roofs. Domino's built the delivery machine, fixed its pizza, and won the phone. Now look at what that did to Pizza Hut's buildings.
Chapter five. The wrong buildings, and the bill that came with them.

Here is the choice that cost Pizza Hut its crown. Its empire was built on dine-in restaurants: big buildings, big parking lots, booths and waiters. For a family night out, that was perfect. For a country that orders from the couch, it was a heavy weight.
When Americans stopped sitting down for pizza, Pizza Hut was left holding the buildings. And what do you do with a dining room nobody sits in?
When fewer people sit down, a big dining room doesn't shrink. The rent, the heating and the staff cost the same, even when half the tables are empty.
In 2020, its biggest franchisee in America, NPC International, filed for bankruptcy. It owned 1,227 Pizza Hut locations.
It agreed to close up to 300 of them. And which ones? Pizza Hut said that too.
A substantial majority, it said, were dine-in locations.
So where did Pizza Hut's customers go? Many simply stayed home and ordered. And the chain built for ordering was Domino's. The market share numbers show where the business went.
And the parts of Pizza Hut built for takeout were doing fine. That spring, its delivery and carryout sales rose 21%, not counting closed Express counters.

Pizza Hut had tried to catch up: its own delivery, carryout, and small Pizza Hut Express counters inside Target stores. But changing direction is slow when you are carrying thousands of old buildings.
But the sales kept falling. Pizza Hut's sales at existing stores fell for 10 quarters in a row. In 2025 alone, they dropped 5%.
Inside Yum, Pizza Hut had become the small one. KFC and Taco Bell made roughly 90% of the group's divisional profit, its finance chief said.
In the first quarter of 2026, Pizza Hut's core operating profit fell 14%. And America, where it was losing, was 40% of its sales.
Then Domino's came for the one thing Pizza Hut invented. In 2025, it launched its own Stuffed Crust, despite Pizza Hut's head start of 30 years.
Domino's own filing credits the Parmesan Stuffed Crust with lifting its US sales.
By now, Pizza Hut's owner was asking a question it had never asked before. Should it keep Pizza Hut at all? And if not, who would buy it?
Chapter six. For sale: the day Pizza Hut's owner decided to let go.
In 2025, Yum Brands began a review of its options for Pizza Hut. What did that mean? A sale was one possibility.
In February, it decided to close about 250 underperforming Pizza Huts in the United States.
At the start of 2026, about 6,300 Pizza Huts were left in America, down from more than 8,600 in 1997.
Domino's, meanwhile, had 7,186 stores in America. The chain with no dining rooms now had more restaurants in the country than the king. How did that happen? One small store at a time.
That's 1,500 more closings than openings in ten years.
Yum's chief executive said a turnaround might be best done outside the company.
The contrast inside Yum was stark. KFC's operating profit grew through 2025 and into the next year. Pizza Hut's was shrinking.
So in June 2026, Yum agreed to sell Pizza Hut in two deals, worth $2.7B together.
A private equity firm, LongRange Capital, paid $1.5B for Pizza Hut outside China. Yum China paid $1.2B for the business in mainland China.
Why two buyers? Because there were really two Pizza Huts: one struggling in America and much of the world, and one in China that people still lined up to sit in.
Both deals closed by September. Yum, Pizza Hut's owner since 1997, had let it go.
What Yum sold wasn't only restaurants. It was a name people had grown up with: the red roof, BOOK IT!, and the original Stuffed Crust.
The red roof had a new owner, and a smaller future in America. But there's one country where the story runs the other way. Where do people still want to sit down at a Pizza Hut?
Chapter seven. The one country where the red roof still wins.
Pizza Hut opened its first restaurant in China in 1990, in Beijing. How did a chain from Kansas end up there?
There, it is a sit-down restaurant from breakfast to dinner, with pasta and steak on the menu beside the pizza.
By the end of 2025, there were 4,168 Pizza Huts in China, in over a thousand cities.
Its operator calls it the largest casual dining brand in China. The same dine-in model that struggled in America became a winner there.
And it hasn't stood still there. Yum China says robot servers now work in over 60% of its Pizza Hut restaurants.
Yum China already ran those restaurants. With the sale, it owns the Pizza Hut business there outright.
Worldwide, Domino's also has more restaurants. At the close of 2025, Pizza Hut counted 19,974 in total. Domino's had more than 22,100.
Domino's now calls itself the largest pizza company in the world.
Chapter eight. What really happened, and what it teaches.

Put the whole war on one line. Pizza Hut opens in Wichita. Two years later, the Monaghans buy a store in Ypsilanti. Domino's drops its guarantee, fixes its recipe, takes the lead, and Pizza Hut is sold.
Pizza Hut's next chapter now belongs to a private equity firm, and its future in America depends on how many red roofs it can afford to keep.
Pizza Hut didn't lose because people stopped wanting pizza. America kept eating it. People just stopped sitting down for it. The record shows it in the closures, in the filings, and in the sale.
Every change in how people ordered, the phone, the website, the app, made Domino's model stronger, and made Pizza Hut's buildings heavier.
So did Domino's beat Pizza Hut, or did the way people eat? The honest answer is both. Domino's saw where eating was going, and built for it before anyone else.
Pizza Hut fell from 16.9% to 12.1%. Domino's climbed from 14.2% all the way up to 23.4%. In ten years, Domino's held nearly twice Pizza Hut's share.
So what's the lesson? First: the thing that made you king can become the thing that holds you down. The red roofs were Pizza Hut's signature, and then its biggest bill.
Second: saying out loud that your product is bad can be the best ad you ever run. Domino's told the truth about its pizza, fixed it, and grew.
And third: a better recipe can't save the wrong model. Pizza Hut invented Stuffed Crust. Domino's launched its own, and it was Domino's sales that rose.
Now we want to hear from you. Red roof or blue box: which one did you grow up on, and do you still sit down for pizza?
Thanks for watching this story, told from the public record.
